evidence: src/modules/identity/core/application/usecases/address/set-default-address/set-default-address.usecase.ts: `@Injectable()` on `SetDefaultAddressUseCase` is NestJS framework dependency-injection wiring. This belongs to the application or infrastructure layer, not domain.

`execute()` calls `this.userRepository.findByIdForUpdate(userId)` and then `this.userRepository.save(user, expectedVersion)`. Coordinating a load and save with optimistic locking is application-layer work.
`execute()` runs the `OwnedResourceAccessPolicy.canMutateResource(callerContext, ...)` authorization check before loading. Gating access on the caller is application-layer work.
The class extends `UseCase<SetDefaultAddressInput, void, UseCaseError>` and returns `UseCaseError`, which marks it as an application use case, not a domain entity, value object or service.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: This file is declared as domain because its path contains `/core/`. It is really an application use case, as its `/application/usecases/` path and `.usecase.ts` suffix show. `SetDefaultAddressUseCase.execute` coordinates a full transaction. It runs an access-policy check, loads the aggregate through `userRepository.findByIdForUpdate`, delegates to `user.setDefaultAddress`, and saves through `userRepository.save(user, expectedVersion)` with an optimistic-concurrency version. That is application-layer coordination, not domain behaviour. The class also carries the NestJS `@Injectable()` decorator, which is framework dependency-injection wiring. A domain file should not hold either responsibility. The business rule itself stays in the entity (`user.setDefaultAddress`), so there is no misplaced business logic. The problem is that the file's responsibilities match the application layer, not the declared domain layer. The mismatch probably comes from the layer patterns overlapping, but under the given model it still breaks the rule.
